name: Ostrich Effect
description: People sometimes avoid looking at information when they expect it to be unpleasant, threatening, or discouraging. Bad news is easier to postpone by not opening the dashboard, statement, or result at all.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to finance, health, safety, and account-status products: users may avoid debt dashboards, abnormal test results, privacy warnings, or performance reports when the UI is likely to confirm something negative.
prevalence_note: Known in behavioral finance and occasionally in health/information-avoidance discussions, but not a mainstream named heuristic in ordinary product-design critique.

findings.description: An fMRI study found the brain's mesolimbic reward circuitry selectively treats the opportunity to learn favorable future outcomes as rewarding, but not unfavorable ones -- explaining why people seek knowledge about desirable outcomes more than undesirable ones, and pay to remain ignorant of undesirable ones. Directly explains ostrich-effect-relevant real-world behavior: rejecting medical screenings and monitoring investments more during bull than bear markets. Independently confirms the ostrich effect via a completely different method (neuroimaging) and identifies its underlying neural mechanism, which the corpus's existing finance-domain evidence didn't have.
findings.source_title: Valuation of knowledge and ignorance in mesolimbic reward circuitry
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

findings.description: In two investor datasets from Scandinavia and the United States, investors monitored their portfolios more frequently in rising markets than in flat or falling markets, consistent with selective avoidance of potentially bad financial news after adverse prior information.
findings.source_title: The ostrich effect: Selective attention to information
